title: Common Changes, Simple Support, and When to Reach Out
learningGoals: Use simple, everyday steps that may ease nausea, and know when to ask for more help
Know that bleeding in early pregnancy is common but always worth a call, and which signs need a call right away
Recognize urgent maternal warning signs and get care right away
Know a few healthy habits for early pregnancy

slides.heading: Common Changes, Simple Support, and When to Reach Out
onScreen: Early Pregnancy Basics · Lesson 2
About 10 minutes
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson, we'll talk about the changes many people notice in the first trimester, and simple things that may help. Then we'll talk about something just as important: knowing when to reach out to your care team, and when to get help right away. You don't have to memorize everything. You'll be able to save the key parts to your Birth Readiness Brief. Let's begin.

visual.description: Two expecting parents of different backgrounds sitting on a sunny porch step, one holding a water bottle, talking and smiling. Soft coral and sage colors.

slides.heading: Changes many people notice
onScreen: Sore or tender breasts
Feeling more tired than usual
Nausea, food cravings, or food dislikes
Peeing more often, mood swings, headaches
slides.narration: Your body is doing a lot of work right now, and hormones are changing fast. Many people notice sore or tender breasts. You may feel more tired than usual. Nausea is common. So are sudden food cravings, or suddenly disliking a food you used to love. You may need to pee more often. Your moods may swing up and down. And some people get headaches early on. Not everyone has all of these, and that's okay too. Every pregnancy is different.

visual.description: A soft illustrated checklist of everyday changes with gentle icons: a pillow, a plate, a water drop, a cloud with sun peeking through. Pastel lavender and peach.

slides.heading: Simple support for nausea
onScreen: Eat small "mini meals" through the day
Try bland foods, and add some protein
Drink throughout the day, not just when thirsty
Avoid smells that set you off
slides.narration: Nausea usually starts before nine weeks, and for most people it eases by about fourteen weeks. Until then, small changes can help. Try eating five or six mini meals a day, so your stomach is never empty. Keep crackers by your bed and eat a few before you get up. Bland foods, like bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast, are often easier to keep down. Try to add a little protein, like yogurt, nuts, or nut butter, to each meal. Sip fluids throughout the day, not just when you feel thirsty. If a bad taste makes water hard to drink, chewing gum or sucking on hard candy may help. And if certain smells bother you, use a fan when cooking, or ask someone else to take out the trash.

visual.description: A small plate with crackers, banana slices, and yogurt beside a water glass, with a kitchen fan in the background. Soft yellow and mint tones.

slides.heading: When nausea needs more help
onScreen: Nausea is affecting your daily life or worrying you
Safe treatment options exist
Ask your team before trying any medicine or supplement
slides.narration: For some people, nausea is mild and passes. For others, it's much harder, and it can get in the way of work, sleep, and daily life. If nausea is affecting your life or worrying you, talk with your care team. There are safe treatments that can help you feel better and keep it from getting worse. Your team will first make sure nothing else is causing it. Then they'll help you choose what's right for you. Please don't start a medicine, vitamin, or herbal remedy for nausea on your own. Check with your care team first.

visual.description: A person on a video call with a friendly clinician, notebook open on their lap. Diverse, warm and soft blue tones.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: Let's pause for a quick check-in.

question.prompt: A friend says ginger candy and a sleep aid fixed her nausea. What's the best next step for you?
options: Ask your care team which options are right for you
Stop eating until the nausea passes
question.explanation: What helped a friend may not be right for you. Your care team can check for other causes and help you pick safe options. In the meantime, small frequent meals and sipping fluids may help.

slides.heading: Bleeding in early pregnancy
onScreen: Bleeding in the first trimester is common
Often it isn't a sign of a major problem
Spotting can happen after sex or a pelvic exam
Still, call your care team about any bleeding
slides.narration: Seeing blood when you're pregnant can be scary. So let's talk about it calmly. Bleeding in the first trimester is common. It happens in about fifteen to twenty-five out of every one hundred pregnancies. In many cases, it isn't a sign of a major problem. Light spotting can happen when the pregnancy first settles into the uterus. Your cervix, the opening of your uterus, can also bleed more easily now, so spotting after sex or after a pelvic exam isn't unusual. But bleeding can also be a sign of a problem that needs care. So the rule is simple. Call your care team about any bleeding during pregnancy.

visual.description: A calm person sitting on the edge of a bed holding a phone, about to make a call, with soft morning light. Muted rose and gray palette.

slides.heading: Bleeding: when to call right away
onScreen: Bleeding with belly, pelvic, or shoulder pain: call right away
Bleeding more than spotting, like a period: get care now
Weakness or fainting: get care now
Tell them you're pregnant
slides.narration: Some bleeding needs attention right away. If you have bleeding along with pain in your belly, your pelvis, or your shoulder, call your care team right away. These can be signs of a pregnancy growing outside the uterus, which needs care quickly. If you're bleeding more than spotting, like a period, get medical care right away. And if you feel weak or you faint, get care right away. When you call or arrive, tell them you're pregnant.

slides.heading: Common changes vs. call your care team
onScreen: Left: often common. Right: call your care team.
When in doubt, call. That's what your team is there for.
slides.narration: Here's a side-by-side guide. On the left are changes that are common. On the right are signs that mean you should call your care team. Nausea that comes and goes is common. But if you can't keep food or fluids down, or you're losing weight, call. Feeling tired is common. Feeling dizzy or faint when you stand, or having a racing heartbeat, means call. Peeing more often is common. Peeing only a little, and it's dark, means call. A headache early on can be common. A headache that won't go away or keeps getting worse is a warning sign. Spotting can happen. And any bleeding is worth a call. These are guides, not hard rules. If something doesn't feel right, reach out.
rows: Can't keep food or fluids down, or losing weight
Dizzy or faint when standing, or a racing heartbeat
Only a small amount of dark urine
A headache that won't go away or gets worse
Any bleeding (call right away if there's pain too)

visual.description: Two-column table with soft color coding: left column in calm sage, right column in warm amber with a small phone icon.

slides.heading: Urgent warning signs: get care right away
onScreen: Headache that won't go away, vision changes, or fainting
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast-beating heart
Severe belly pain or severe vomiting
Fever of 100.4°F or higher, or extreme swelling
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
slides.narration: Some signs need medical care right away, at any point in pregnancy. Get care right away if you have a headache that won't go away or gets worse, changes in your vision, or dizziness or fainting. Get care for trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast-beating heart. Get care for severe belly pain that doesn't go away. And for severe vomiting, where you can't drink for more than eight hours, or eat for more than twenty-four hours. Other urgent signs are a fever of one hundred point four degrees or higher, extreme swelling of your hands or face, severe swelling, redness, or pain in a leg or arm, overwhelming tiredness, and bleeding more than spotting. And if you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, reach out for help right away. Always tell them you're pregnant. If something just doesn't feel right, trust yourself and reach out.

question.prompt: At seven weeks, you notice light bleeding along with pain in your shoulder. What should you do?
options: Wait a few days to see if it stops
Call your care team right away
Mention it at your next routine visit
question.explanation: Bleeding with belly, pelvic, or shoulder pain needs a call right away. It can be a sign of a pregnancy outside the uterus, which needs fast care. If you feel weak or faint, get medical care right away.

slides.heading: How to call about a symptom
onScreen: Say you're pregnant and how far along
Say what you feel and when it started
If something isn't right, say so
slides.narration: Knowing what to say can make calling easier. Watch this short example.

video.brief: A pregnant person calls their clinic's nurse line while a support person sits beside them. They say: 'I'm about eight weeks pregnant.' They describe the symptom, when it started, and how it has changed, then say: 'Something doesn't feel right to me.' On-screen caption repeats: Tell them you're pregnant. Describe what you feel. Trust yourself. No clinical thresholds or diagnoses stated.

slides.heading: Healthy habits for now
onScreen: Keep up 400 mcg of folic acid a day
No alcohol: there's no known safe amount
Check with your team before any medicine
Keep your prenatal visits
slides.narration: A few healthy habits go a long way right now. Keep getting four hundred micrograms of folic acid every day. Skip alcohol. There's no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy, and no safe time to drink. That includes wine and beer. If you drank before you knew you were pregnant, stop now and talk with your care team. It's never too late to stop. Check with your team before starting or stopping any medicine, vitamin, or supplement. And keep up with your prenatal checkups.

visual.description: Four soft icons in a row: a vitamin bottle, a sparkling water glass, a phone with a speech bubble, and a calendar. Gentle teal and cream palette.

slides.heading: Your contact plan
onScreen: Your care team's daytime number
Who to call after hours
What they want you to call about
slides.narration: Let's make it easy to reach out when you need to. Write down your care team's daytime number, and who to call after hours. If you haven't asked yet, ask your team which symptoms they want to hear about, and where to go if you need care right away. Save it here in your Birth Readiness Brief, so it's ready when you need it.
slides.prompt: Write your care team's daytime and after-hours numbers, and anything they told you about when to call or where to go for urgent care.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Tiredness, tender breasts, and nausea are common
Small meals and steady sips may ease nausea
Call about any bleeding; with pain, call right away
Urgent warning signs mean get care now
Folic acid yes, alcohol no
slides.narration: Nice work. Let's recap. Changes like tiredness, tender breasts, and nausea are common in the first trimester. Small meals, bland foods, and steady sips of fluid may help with nausea. Ask your care team before trying any medicine or supplement. Call your care team about any bleeding, and call right away if there's pain too. Urgent warning signs mean get care right away, and tell them you're pregnant. And keep up your folic acid, and skip alcohol. Next, a few review questions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which of these is a common first-trimester change?
reviewQuiz.explanation: Tiredness is very common early in pregnancy. A fever of 100.4°F or higher and chest pain are urgent warning signs that need care right away.

reviewQuiz.prompt: You notice light spotting at nine weeks, with no pain. What should you do?
options: Call your care team and let them know
Go for a long run to see if it stops
reviewQuiz.explanation: Spotting is common in early pregnancy and often isn't a sign of a major problem. Still, call your care team about any bleeding. If there's pain, weakness, or heavy bleeding, get care right away.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which is true about alcohol during pregnancy?
options: A glass of wine a day is safe
There's no known safe amount or safe time to drink
reviewQuiz.explanation: The CDC says there's no known safe amount of alcohol and no safe time to drink during pregnancy. All types, including wine and beer, can be harmful. It's never too late to stop.
